| Script    | Runs                          | What it does                                                                                    |
| --------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dev`     | `vite`                        | Starts the dev server with the game server inside it, on port 8080                              |
| `build`   | `oxlint && tsc && vite build` | Lints, type-checks, then builds the game into `dist/client/` and the server into `dist/server/` |
| `preview` | `node dist/server/server.mjs` | Runs the production server, which serves the game and the rooms on port 8080                    |

`start` runs `dev`. In JavaScript projects, `build` skips `tsc`.

## The game and the server in one process

`vite.config.ts` adds the Colyseus [Vite plugin](https://docs.colyseus.io/server/vite):

```ts title="vite.config.ts"
import { colyseus } from "colyseus/vite";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

// The dev server and the built game server both listen on this port
const port = 8080;

// https://vite.dev/config/
export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    // Runs the game server inside the dev server. The build writes it to
    // dist/server/server.mjs, which also serves the game from dist/client.
    colyseus({ serverEntry: "/server/index.ts", port, serveClient: true }),
  ],
  server: {
    port,
    open: true,
    // Lets other people reach the dev server through a cloudflared tunnel
    allowedHosts: [".trycloudflare.com"],
  },
  build: {
    // PixiJS, PixiJS 3D and the game libraries together are larger than
    // Vite's 500 kB default
    chunkSizeWarningLimit: 1000,
  },
  environments: {
    // The game server serves public/ from dist/client, so skip a second copy
    colyseus: { build: { copyPublicDir: false } },
  },
});
```

`allowedHosts` lets the dev server answer requests that come through a [cloudflared](https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflared) quick tunnel, which gives it a public HTTPS address. You can use one to [play with friends](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/web.md#play-with-friends) on your dev server, and the [Discord platform](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md#test-inside-discord) runs the game inside Discord this way.

In development, `npm run dev` starts one process. Vite serves the game, and the plugin runs the server from `server/index.ts` on the same port, so there's no second terminal and no proxy. When you save a file in `src/`, the page reloads. When you save a file in `server/`, the plugin reloads the server code without restarting the process. Rooms keep their state, and open pages reconnect on their own, so bunnies stay where they were. A file that both the game and the server import, such as `server/world.ts`, reloads the pages too. Their old bunnies stay for about 15 seconds, until the room gives up on the old connections. If a page shows "Can't reach the game server", refresh it.

`vite build` builds two things: the game into `dist/client/`, and a standalone server into `dist/server/server.mjs`. With `serveClient: true`, that server also serves the files in `dist/client/`, so one Node.js process runs the whole game.

## How state sync works

### The state

`server/GameState.ts` describes the state with `schema()` from `@colyseus/schema`:

```ts title="server/GameState.ts"
import { schema, t } from "@colyseus/schema";
import type { SchemaType } from "@colyseus/schema";

/**
 * A player's bunny. The server sets its position, and its name when players
 * sign in.
 */
export const Player = schema(
  { x: t.number(), y: t.number(), name: t.string() },
  "Player",
);

/** The room state. Every change is sent to every player in the room. */
export const GameState = schema({ players: t.map(Player) }, "GameState");
export type GameState = SchemaType<typeof GameState>;
```

`players` is a map from each player's session id to their `Player`. Only fields declared here are synced. Colyseus sends just the fields that changed, 20 times a second by default, in a compact binary format.

### The room

`server/GameRoom.ts` is the only code that changes the state:

```ts title="server/GameRoom.ts"
import { Room } from "colyseus";
import type { Client } from "colyseus";

import { GameState, Player } from "./GameState.ts";
import { onAuth } from "./platform.ts";
import type { JoinOptions } from "./platform.ts";
import { WORLD_HEIGHT, WORLD_WIDTH } from "./world.ts";

/** Every player who joins gets a bunny they can move and make jump */
export class GameRoom extends Room<{ state: GameState }> {
  /** Signs players in on platforms that need it, before they join */
  static onAuth = onAuth;

  state = new GameState();

  messages = {
    move: (client: Client, message: { x: number; y: number }) => {
      const player = this.state.players.get(client.sessionId);

      // Clients can send anything, so check the message before using it
      if (
        !player ||
        !Number.isFinite(message?.x) ||
        !Number.isFinite(message?.y)
      ) {
        return;
      }

      player.x = clamp(message.x, 0, WORLD_WIDTH);
      player.y = clamp(message.y, 0, WORLD_HEIGHT);
    },
    jump: (client: Client) => {
      this.broadcast("jump", client.sessionId);
    },
  };

  /** The options src/connect.ts joins with, already checked by onAuth */
  onJoin(client: Client<{ auth?: { name: string } }>, _options?: JoinOptions) {
    // Reloading the dev server rejoins every player into the restored room
    if (this.state.players.has(client.sessionId)) return;

    this.state.players.set(
      client.sessionId,
      new Player({
        x: Math.random() * WORLD_WIDTH,
        y: Math.random() * WORLD_HEIGHT,
        // Templates that sign players in, like Discord, set client.auth
        name: client.auth?.name ?? "",
      }),
    );
  }

  onLeave(client: Client) {
    this.state.players.delete(client.sessionId);
  }

  /** Without this, an error in the room stops the whole server */
  onUncaughtException(error: Error) {
    console.error(error);
  }
}

function clamp(value: number, min: number, max: number) {
  return Math.min(Math.max(value, min), max);
}
```

- `onJoin` adds a `Player` at a random spot when someone joins, and `onLeave` removes it when they leave. After a dev server reload, players join the restored room again, so `onJoin` keeps a bunny that's already there. The player's `name` comes from `client.auth`, which the platform's `onAuth` sets. On the web it doesn't, so `name` stays empty.
- `messages` handles what players send. `move` ignores anything that isn't a pair of numbers and keeps the bunny on the floor, so a modified client can't send its bunny off the floor. Use `client.sessionId` to know who sent a message, never an id from the message itself.
- `jump` isn't state. Nothing needs to remember that a bunny jumped, so the room passes it on to every player with `broadcast` instead.
- `onUncaughtException` logs errors thrown in the room's code, so one bug doesn't take the server down for everyone.

`server/index.ts` registers the room under the name `game`:

```ts title="server/index.ts"
import { defineRoom, defineServer } from "colyseus";

import { GameRoom } from "./GameRoom.ts";
import { filterBy, routes } from "./platform.ts";

export const server = defineServer({
  rooms: {
    // The platform can split players into separate rooms, as Discord does
    // with one room per Activity session
    game: defineRoom(GameRoom).filterBy(filterBy),
  },
  routes,
});
```

### How platforms change the server

`onAuth`, `JoinOptions`, `filterBy` and `routes` come from `server/platform.ts`, which belongs to the platform. They're how the same room works on every platform:

| Export        | What it does                                                       | Web                              | Discord                                                      |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `onAuth`      | Runs before a player joins. What it returns becomes `client.auth`. | Lets everyone in                 | Lets in only players signed in with Discord, with their name |
| `JoinOptions` | The options `src/connect.ts` joins with, so TypeScript checks them | None                             | The Activity session's `instanceId`                          |
| `filterBy`    | Join options that split players into separate rooms                | None, so everyone joins one room | `instanceId`, so each Activity session gets its own room     |
| `routes`      | HTTP routes the server adds                                        | None                             | `/api/token`, which trades a sign-in code for a token        |

See the [web](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/web.md#multiplayer) and [Discord](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md#multiplayer) platforms for their versions of the file.

### The game

`src/connect.ts` exports `joinGame()`, which joins the `game` room. On the web it's one call to `joinOrCreate("game")`; on Discord it also sends the token of the player `initPlatform` signed in, and the Activity session's id. Either way, the scene doesn't change. See [the web's `src/connect.ts`](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/web.md#multiplayer).

`src/scene.ts` calls `joinGame()` and reacts to state changes with `Callbacks` from `@colyseus/sdk`:

```ts title="src/scene.ts"
const room = await joinGame();
const callbacks = Callbacks.get(room);
const players = new Map<string, Container>();

status.text = "";

callbacks.onAdd("players", (player, sessionId) => {
  const view = createPlayer(sessionId === room.sessionId, player.name);

  view.position.set(player.x, player.y);
  players.set(sessionId, view);
  world.addChild(view);

  const stopWalking = callbacks.onChange(player, () =>
    walk(view, player.x, player.y),
  );

  // Without this, a dev server reload can try to move a removed bunny
  view.once("destroyed", stopWalking);
});

const removePlayer = (sessionId: string) => {
  const view = players.get(sessionId)!;

  players.delete(sessionId);
  gsap.killTweensOf([view, ...view.children]);
  view.destroy({ children: true });
};

callbacks.onRemove("players", (_player, sessionId) => removePlayer(sessionId));
```

- The local `players` map holds the bunny drawn for each session id, so later callbacks can find it.
- `onAdd` runs for every player already in the room and for each one who joins later, including you. Your own bunny gets the glow. `createPlayer` also draws the player's `name` above the bunny. On the web `name` is empty, so no label shows.
- `onChange` runs when the server changes a player's `x` or `y`. It returns a function that stops listening, which the scene calls when it destroys the bunny.
- `onRemove` runs when a player leaves.

If the connection drops, the SDK tries to reconnect on its own, and the scene shows "Reconnecting..." until it succeeds or "Disconnected" if it can't. The room removes a player as soon as they disconnect, so apart from server reloads in development, a player who drops has to reload the page to play again. When the game leaves the room, the scene removes every bunny.

Clicking the floor sends a `move` message with the spot you clicked. The bunny doesn't move until the server answers with a new position. `walk` then tweens it there with GSAP at a steady speed, which also smooths over the gaps between updates:

```ts title="src/scene.ts"
function walk(view: Container, x: number, y: number) {
  gsap.to(view, {
    x,
    y,
    duration: Math.hypot(x - view.x, y - view.y) / SPEED,
    ease: "none",
    overwrite: true,
  });
}
```

`Client<typeof server>` in `connect.ts` imports the server's type, so TypeScript checks room names, and `player` in the scene's callbacks has the fields from the schema. The import is type-only, so no server code ends up in the game bundle. The game does import `server/world.ts`, which holds plain numbers.

The floor's size is set in world units in `server/world.ts`. The scene scales the floor to fit the screen, so a position means the same spot for every player, whatever their screen size.

## Run the production build

```bash
npm run build
npm run preview
```

Then open <http://localhost:8080>. `preview` runs `dist/server/server.mjs` with Node.js. It's the same server you deploy.

## Deploy

A multiplayer game needs a host that runs Node.js and accepts WebSocket connections. A static host can serve `dist/client/`, but the game can't connect without the server.

`dist/server/server.mjs` loads `colyseus`, `express` and the other dependencies from `node_modules` instead of bundling them. On the server:

1. Copy `dist/`, `package.json` and your lockfile.
2. Install the dependencies without the dev tools, for example with `npm ci --omit=dev`. This still comes to about 380 MB, mostly `uWebSockets.js`.
3. Run `node dist/server/server.mjs`, or `npm run preview`.

The server listens on `port` from `vite.config.ts`, 8080 by default. The build writes the port into `dist/server/server.mjs`, so to use another one, change it and build again. The server doesn't read the `PORT` environment variable. A host that picks the port when the server starts and passes it in `PORT` needs `PORT` set to your port; if the host doesn't let you choose it, the built server can't run there as it is.

The server answers any path it has no file for with `index.html`, so a missing asset in production loads as HTML and fails to decode instead of returning a 404.

The [Colyseus deployment guide](https://docs.colyseus.io/deployment) covers process managers, scaling to more than one process, and Colyseus Cloud. A Discord Activity also needs HTTPS and its Discord settings; see [deploy a Discord Activity](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md#deploy).

## Change the game

- **Sync more data**: add a field to `Player` or `GameState`, such as `score: t.number()`, and set it in the room. The game sees it in `onChange`. See [schema types](https://docs.colyseus.io/state/schema).
- **Show player names**: on the web, pass a name in `joinOrCreate("game", { name })` in `src/connect.ts`, change `JoinOptions` in `server/platform.ts` to `{ name: string }`, and use `options.name` for the new `Player`'s `name` in the room's `onJoin`. The scene draws it above the bunny. Check that it's a short string first, as `move` checks its message. The [Discord platform](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md#multiplayer) takes the name from the player's Discord account instead.
- **Send another action**: add a handler to `messages` in the room and call `room.send()` from the game.
- **Limit message spam**: set `maxMessagesPerSecond` on the room to disconnect a client that sends more messages than that.
- **Limit players**: set `maxClients` on the room. When a room is full, `joinOrCreate` opens a new one.
- **Keep a player's seat after a dropped connection**: the template removes a player as soon as they disconnect. Colyseus can hold the seat while the game reconnects. See [reconnection](https://docs.colyseus.io/room/reconnection).

## Learn more

- [Colyseus documentation](https://docs.colyseus.io), including [state sync callbacks](https://docs.colyseus.io/state/callbacks), [rooms](https://docs.colyseus.io/room) and the [client SDK](https://docs.colyseus.io/sdk).
- [Client prediction](https://docs.colyseus.io/netcode/client-prediction), to move your own bunny before the server answers.
- [Game templates](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/games.md) for the libraries the game uses.

---

# Bundler templates

The bundler templates are the smallest starting point: a PixiJS `Application`, a spinning bunny in front of a spinning [3D](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/pixijs-3d.md) cube, and a build setup. All four run the same code. They differ in how that code reaches the browser.

**npm**

```bash
npm create pixi.js@latest my-app -- --template bundler-vite
```

**yarn**

```bash
yarn create pixi.js my-app --template bundler-vite
```

**pnpm**

```bash
pnpm create pixi.js my-app --template bundler-vite
```

**bun**

```bash
bun create pixi.js my-app --template bundler-vite
```

Swap `bundler-vite` for `bundler-webpack`, `bundler-esbuild` or `bundler-import-map`, and add `-js` for the JavaScript version of the first three.

## Project structure

This is the Vite template in TypeScript:

```text
my-app/
├── .vscode/
│   ├── extensions.json
│   └── settings.json
├── public/
│   ├── assets/
│   │   └── bunny.png
│   ├── favicon.png
│   └── style.css
├── src/
│   ├── main.ts
│   └── vite-env.d.ts
├── .gitignore
├── .oxfmtrc.json
├── .oxlintrc.json
├── index.html
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
└── vite.config.ts
```

The other templates change a few files:

- webpack has `webpack.config.mjs` in place of `vite.config.ts` and `src/vite-env.d.ts`.
- esbuild has `scripts/dev.mjs` and `scripts/build.mjs`, and keeps `index.html` in `public/`.
- Import map has no bundler config and no TypeScript. Its code is in `src/main.js`, and `index.html` holds the import map.

`index.html` has a `#pixi-container` element inside `#app`, and `public/style.css` makes `#app` fill the window. `src/main.ts` creates the app, a [PixiJS 3D](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/pixijs-3d.md) view with a lit cube, and the bunny:

```ts title="src/main.ts"
import {
  CubeGeometry,
  DirectionalLight,
  Material3D,
  Mesh3D,
  View3D,
} from "@pixi/3d";
import { Application, Assets, Sprite } from "pixi.js";

const app = new Application();

await app.init({ background: "#1099bb", resizeTo: window, antialias: true });
document.getElementById("pixi-container")!.appendChild(app.canvas);

// A View3D draws a 3D scene. autoResize makes it fill the screen.
const view = new View3D({
  autoResize: true,
  // Soft light from the sky above and the ground below
  environment: { skyColor: 0xc9d6ff, groundColor: 0x3a2f45 },
});

const cube = new Mesh3D({
  geometry: new CubeGeometry(),
  material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xe72264 }),
});

// A directional light works like the sun: only its direction matters.
// This one shines down on the cube from the upper left.
const sun = new DirectionalLight({ intensity: 3 });

sun.position.set(-3, 5, 2);
sun.lookAt(cube.position);

view.root.addChild(cube, sun);
view.camera.position.set(0, 1.6, 3);
view.camera.lookAt(cube.position);

const texture = await Assets.load("assets/bunny.png");
const bunny = new Sprite(texture);

bunny.anchor.set(0.5);

// Center the bunny, and keep it centered when the window resizes
bunny.position.set(app.screen.width / 2, app.screen.height / 2);
app.renderer.on("resize", (width, height) => {
  bunny.position.set(width / 2, height / 2);
});

// The bunny is added after the view, so it draws in front of the cube
app.stage.addChild(view, bunny);

// deltaTime keeps the speed the same at any frame rate
app.ticker.add((time) => {
  cube.rotation.y += 0.01 * time.deltaTime;
  bunny.rotation += 0.1 * time.deltaTime;
});
```

## Scripts

| Script    | Vite           | webpack                            | esbuild                  | Import map              |
| --------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------- |
| `dev`     | `vite`         | `webpack serve --mode=development` | `node scripts/dev.mjs`   | `http-server . -o -c-1` |
| `build`   | `vite build`   | `webpack --mode=production`        | `node scripts/build.mjs` | none                    |
| `preview` | `vite preview` | `webpack serve --mode=production`  | none                     | none                    |

`start` runs `dev`. `lint` runs oxlint and `format` runs oxfmt, as described in [linting and formatting](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/linting-and-formatting.md).

In TypeScript templates, `build` first runs `oxlint`, then `tsc` to type-check, then the bundler. A lint error or a type error stops the build. JavaScript templates skip the `tsc` step. Every build writes to `dist/`.

## Static assets

Put images, sounds, fonts and other files in `public/`. The dev server serves them next to `index.html`, and the build copies them into `dist/` unchanged. `public/assets/bunny.png` loads like this:

```ts
const texture = await Assets.load("assets/bunny.png");
```

The import map template serves the whole project folder, so the same file is at `./public/assets/bunny.png`.

Code in the templates loads files with paths that don't start with `/`, and the Vite templates set `base: "./"`, so a build works from any folder, such as a GitHub Pages project site at `/my-app/`. In your own code, a path that starts with `/` resolves from the domain root.

## Change the dev server port

Every template uses port 8080.

| Template   | Where the port is set                                     | One-off override             |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Vite       | `server.port` in `vite.config.ts`                         | `npm run dev -- --port 3000` |
| webpack    | `devServer.port` in `webpack.config.mjs`                  | `npm run dev -- --port 3000` |
| esbuild    | `port` in the `context.serve()` call in `scripts/dev.mjs` | none                         |
| Import map | add `-p 3000` to the `dev` script in `package.json`       | `npm run dev -- -p 3000`     |

With yarn, pnpm and bun, leave out the `--`, for example `pnpm dev --port 3000`.

In the [multiplayer](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/multiplayer.md) game templates, change `const port` in `vite.config.ts`. It sets the dev server port and the production server's port. The single-player [Discord](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md#deploy) template's production server listens on the `PORT` environment variable instead, or 8080 without it.

## Vite

[Vite](https://vite.dev) serves your source files directly in development, so the dev server starts at once and the page updates when you save. It's the recommended template.

```ts title="vite.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

// https://vite.dev/config/
export default defineConfig({
  // Relative URLs so the build works from any folder, e.g. GitHub Pages
  base: "./",
  server: {
    port: 8080,
    open: true,
  },
});
```

`base: "./"` makes the built files reference each other with relative URLs. `open: true` opens the browser when the dev server starts. After `npm run build`, run `npm run preview` to serve `dist/` locally and check the production build.

Vite can import any file as a string with the `?raw` suffix, which is how you load GLSL shaders. See [importing shader files](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/troubleshooting.md#importing-glsl-shader-files).

## webpack

The webpack template uses [webpack](https://webpack.js.org) 5 with [esbuild-loader](https://github.com/privatenumber/esbuild-loader) to compile TypeScript and modern JavaScript. esbuild-loader doesn't type-check, which is why `build` runs `tsc` first.

`webpack.config.mjs` sets up:

- `copy-webpack-plugin` to copy `public/` into `dist/`.
- `html-webpack-plugin` to write `dist/index.html` from `index.html` with the bundle script added.
- A content hash in the bundle file name, `[name].[contenthash].js`, so browsers fetch new files after each release.
- Source maps in development only.
- esbuild minification in production.

`npm run preview` serves a production build from memory, so you can check it without a separate server.

> **Production builds remove console calls**
>
> The production minifier is configured with `drop: ["console"]`, so the build removes every `console` call from `dist/`. Remove that option from the `EsbuildPlugin` in `webpack.config.mjs` if you need logs in production.

## esbuild

The esbuild template uses [esbuild](https://esbuild.github.io)'s own API in two short scripts, with no plugins.

- `scripts/dev.mjs` bundles `src/main.ts` in memory, serves `public/` on port 8080, and reloads the page after each rebuild using esbuild's live reload event. Changes to files in `public/` need a manual refresh.
- `scripts/build.mjs` deletes `dist/`, copies `public/` into it, and writes a minified `dist/bundle.js`.

Both scripts output an ES module, so top-level `await` works. `public/index.html` loads `bundle.js`. The dev server doesn't open a browser, so go to <http://localhost:8080> yourself.

## Import map

The import map template has no bundler and no build step. `index.html` tells the browser where to find `pixi.js` and PixiJS 3D:

```html title="index.html"
<script type="importmap">
  {
    "imports": {
      "pixi.js": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pixi.js@8/dist/pixi.min.mjs",
      "@pixi/3d": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@pixi/3d@0.1.0/dist/pixijs-3d.min.mjs",
      "@pixi/3d/extras": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@pixi/3d@0.1.0/dist/pixijs-3d-extras.min.mjs"
    }
  }
</script>
<script type="module" src="./src/main.js"></script>
```

`pixi.js@8` loads the newest 8.x release each time. Pin an exact version, such as `pixi.js@8.23.0`, before you ship so an update can't change your project without warning. `@pixi/3d` is pinned already. Its main file loads its WebGL or WebGPU code from the same folder, and with a version range, a cached main file could load that code from a newer release. Keep both `@pixi/3d` entries on the same version, and both minified or both not. The extras file imports the engine file next to it, so a mismatch loads a second copy of PixiJS 3D.

`npm run dev` runs [http-server](https://github.com/http-party/http-server) on the project folder. `-o` opens the browser and `-c-1` turns off caching. It doesn't reload the page for you, so refresh after you save.

To publish, upload `index.html`, `src/` and `public/`. The browser doesn't load the `pixi.js` and `@pixi/3d` packages from `node_modules`. They're in `package.json` so your editor has their types for autocompletion.

---

# React template

The React template renders PixiJS from React components with [@pixi/react](https://react.pixijs.io). It's built on the [Vite template](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#vite), so the scripts, the `public/` folder and the dev port all work the same way.

**npm**

```bash
npm create pixi.js@latest my-app -- --template framework-react
```

**yarn**

```bash
yarn create pixi.js my-app --template framework-react
```

**pnpm**

```bash
pnpm create pixi.js my-app --template framework-react
```

**bun**

```bash
bun create pixi.js my-app --template framework-react
```

Use `framework-react-js` for JavaScript.

## Project structure

```text
my-app/
├── public/
│   ├── assets/
│   │   └── bunny.png
│   ├── favicon.png
│   └── style.css
├── src/
│   ├── App.tsx
│   ├── main.tsx
│   ├── pixi-react.d.ts
│   └── vite-env.d.ts
├── index.html
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
└── vite.config.ts
```

Config files for oxlint, oxfmt, VS Code and git sit at the root as in every template. `vite.config.ts` adds `@vitejs/plugin-react`, and `src/main.tsx` mounts `<App />` into `#pixi-container`.

## Register PixiJS classes with extend

@pixi/react only knows about the PixiJS classes you pass to `extend`. Each one becomes a JSX element with a `pixi` prefix:

```tsx title="src/App.tsx"
import { extend } from "@pixi/react";
import { Sprite } from "pixi.js";

extend({ Sprite });
```

After this, `<pixiSprite>` is available. Add `Container` to the same call to use `<pixiContainer>`, and so on. Using an element you haven't registered throws an error. Registering only what you use keeps the bundle small.

To draw shapes, register `Graphics` and pass a `draw` callback:

```tsx
import { extend } from "@pixi/react";
import { Graphics } from "pixi.js";
import { useCallback } from "react";

extend({ Graphics });

function Box() {
  const draw = useCallback((graphics: Graphics) => {
    graphics.clear();
    graphics.rect(0, 0, 100, 100).fill(0xe91e63);
  }, []);

  return <pixiGraphics draw={draw} />;
}
```

## Create the app with Application

`<Application>` creates the PixiJS `Application` and its canvas. It takes the same options as `app.init()`:

```tsx title="src/App.tsx"
import { Application } from "@pixi/react";

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Application background="#1099bb" resizeTo={window} antialias>
      <SpinningCube />
      <BunnySprite />
    </Application>
  );
}
```

`antialias` smooths the edges of 3D shapes. Children draw in order, so the bunny draws in front of the cube. Components inside `<Application>` can call `useApplication()` to reach the app. The template uses it to keep the bunny centered on the screen.

## Run code every frame with useTick

`useTick` adds a callback to the app's ticker and removes it when the component unmounts:

```tsx title="src/App.tsx"
import { useApplication, useTick } from "@pixi/react";
import { Assets, Sprite, Texture } from "pixi.js";
import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";

const BunnySprite = () => {
  const { app } = useApplication();
  const spriteRef = useRef<Sprite>(null);
  const [texture, setTexture] = useState(Texture.EMPTY);

  useEffect(() => {
    Assets.load<Texture>("assets/bunny.png").then(setTexture);
  }, []);

  useTick((ticker) => {
    const sprite = spriteRef.current;
    if (!sprite) return;

    sprite.position.set(app.screen.width / 2, app.screen.height / 2);
    sprite.rotation += 0.1 * ticker.deltaTime;
  });

  return <pixiSprite ref={spriteRef} texture={texture} anchor={0.5} />;
};
```

The bunny moves and rotates by changing the sprite through a ref, not through React state. Setting its position every frame keeps it centered after the window resizes. Per-frame changes stay out of React's render cycle, which keeps them fast. If the callback sets React state, wrap it in `useCallback`, because `useTick` re-adds the callback whenever it changes.

## Draw 3D with View3D

The template also passes `View3D` from [PixiJS 3D](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/pixijs-3d.md) to `extend`, which adds `<pixiView3D>`. A `View3D` is a 2D display object that draws a 3D scene, so it goes in JSX like a sprite:

```tsx title="src/App.tsx"
import {
  CubeGeometry,
  DirectionalLight,
  Material3D,
  Mesh3D,
  View3D,
} from "@pixi/3d";
import { extend, useTick } from "@pixi/react";
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

extend({ View3D });

const environment = { skyColor: 0xc9d6ff, groundColor: 0x3a2f45 };

const SpinningCube = () => {
  const viewRef = useRef<View3D>(null);
  const cubeRef = useRef<Mesh3D>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const view = viewRef.current!;
    const cube = new Mesh3D({
      geometry: new CubeGeometry(),
      material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xe72264 }),
    });
    const sun = new DirectionalLight({ intensity: 3 });

    sun.position.set(-3, 5, 2);
    sun.lookAt(cube.position);

    view.root.addChild(cube, sun);
    view.camera.position.set(0, 1.6, 3);
    view.camera.lookAt(cube.position);
    cubeRef.current = cube;

    return () => {
      cubeRef.current = null;
      cube.destroy({ geometry: true, material: true });
      sun.destroy();
    };
  }, []);

  useTick((ticker) => {
    const cube = cubeRef.current;
    if (!cube) return;

    cube.rotation.y += 0.01 * ticker.deltaTime;
  });

  return <pixiView3D ref={viewRef} autoResize environment={environment} />;
};
```

The 3D scene inside the view isn't JSX. Meshes and lights go under `view.root`, which @pixi/react doesn't manage, so the effect builds them and keeps the cube in a ref for `useTick`. Its cleanup destroys them when the component unmounts, and before a hot reload runs the effect again. `destroy` also takes each one out of the view, and the `geometry` and `material` flags destroy the cube's geometry and material too. `autoResize` makes the view fill the screen. [PixiJS 3D](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/pixijs-3d.md) explains the lights and the camera.

In TypeScript, `src/pixi-react.d.ts` adds `pixiView3D` to @pixi/react's element types. Classes from `pixi.js` are typed already, so add a line there only for other classes you pass to `extend`.

## Linting

The React template's oxlint config adds the `react` plugin with three rules: `rules-of-hooks` as an error, and `exhaustive-deps` and `only-export-components` as warnings. See [linting and formatting](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/linting-and-formatting.md).

## Learn more

The [@pixi/react documentation](https://react.pixijs.io) covers custom components, TypeScript types for them, and the other hooks.

---

# Extension template

The extension template is a library project for publishing your own PixiJS plugin, such as a filter, a display object or new methods on existing classes. It uses [PixiJS Extension Scripts](https://github.com/pixijs/extension-scripts), a CLI called `xs` that wraps the build, lint, test, docs and release tools in one dev dependency.

**npm**

```bash
npm create pixi.js@latest my-extension -- --template extension-default
```

**yarn**

```bash
yarn create pixi.js my-extension --template extension-default
```

**pnpm**

```bash
pnpm create pixi.js my-extension --template extension-default
```

**bun**

```bash
bun create pixi.js my-extension --template extension-default
```

The extension template is TypeScript only. It doesn't use oxlint or oxfmt. `xs lint` runs ESLint with the PixiJS config instead.

## Project structure

```text
my-extension/
├── examples/
│   └── index.html
├── src/
│   ├── __tests__/
│   │   └── Rectangle.test.ts
│   └── index.ts
├── .gitignore
├── jest.config.mjs
├── LICENSE
├── README.md
├── package.json
└── tsconfig.json
```

The example in `src/index.ts` adds an `expand` method to PixiJS's `Rectangle` and declares it on the global `PixiMixins` namespace, so TypeScript knows about the new method:

```ts title="src/index.ts"
import { Rectangle } from "pixi.js";

declare global {
  namespace PixiMixins {
    interface Rectangle {
      expand(amount: number): this;
    }
  }
}

Rectangle.prototype.expand = function expand(this: Rectangle, amount: number) {
  this.x -= amount;
  this.y -= amount;
  this.width += amount * 2;
  this.height += amount * 2;

  return this;
};
```

`pixi.js` (`>=8.23.0 <9`) and `@pixi/3d` (`^0.1.0`) are peer dependencies, so your package uses the app's copies instead of shipping its own. Both are dev dependencies too, so the build and the tests have them.

The CLI fills in `name` from the folder name and `author` from your `git config user.name`. Update `description` in `package.json` before you publish.

## Scripts

| Script         | Runs            | What it does                                                                                     |
| -------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `dev`, `start` | `xs serve`      | Rebuilds on change and serves the project on port 8080, opening `examples/`                      |
| `watch`        | `xs watch`      | Rebuilds on change without a server                                                              |
| `build`        | `xs build`      | Cleans, lints, type-checks, then bundles into `lib/` and `dist/`                                 |
| `lint`         | `xs lint`       | Runs ESLint on `src/` and `examples/`                                                            |
| `format`       | `xs lint --fix` | Runs ESLint and fixes what it can                                                                |
| `types`        | `xs types`      | Type-checks the project with TypeScript                                                          |
| `test`         | `xs test`       | Runs the Jest tests in `src/__tests__/` inside Electron, so they have a real browser environment |
| `docs`         | `xs docs`       | Writes API docs from your JSDoc comments into `docs/`                                            |
| `release`      | `xs release`    | Bumps the version, tests, builds, deploys docs to GitHub Pages, publishes to npm and pushes tags |

`xs` commands chain with commas, so `"test": "xs types,test"` runs the type check before the tests.

## Build output

`npm run build` writes two sets of files:

- `lib/` holds ES module (`index.mjs`) and CommonJS (`index.js`) builds plus type declarations. These are what bundlers and Node.js use through `main`, `module`, `types` and `exports` in `package.json`.
- `dist/` holds `extension.mjs`, a single ES module for browsers, set by `extensionConfig` in `package.json`. `examples/index.html` loads it through an import map, with `pixi.js` and `@pixi/3d` from jsDelivr.

PixiJS 3D is only published as ES modules, so there's no bundle for a plain `<script>` tag. `"environments": ["node"]` in `extensionConfig` turns that bundle off.

If your extension doesn't use PixiJS 3D, run `npm uninstall @pixi/3d`, which also removes the peer dependency. Then delete `environments` and add `"bundle": "dist/extension.js"` to `extensionConfig` to build the `<script>` tag bundle again.

Both folders are generated and listed in `.gitignore`. The `files` field in `package.json` limits the npm package to these two folders, plus `package.json`, `README.md` and `LICENSE`.

## Tests on CI

`xs test` runs Jest inside Electron with the config in `jest.config.mjs`. That file is the Extension Scripts default plus a transform for the packages that are only published as ES modules: `earcut`, which PixiJS uses, and `@pixi/3d` and its `meshoptimizer` dependency.

On a Linux CI machine without a display, install `xvfb` and run the tests through it:

```yaml
- run: sudo apt-get install xvfb
- run: xvfb-run --auto-servernum npm test
```

## Publishing

`npm run release` asks which version to bump to, then runs the tests, builds, deploys the docs and examples to the `gh-pages` branch, publishes to npm and pushes the git tags. You need to be logged in to npm (`npm login`) and have a GitHub remote.

The [Extension Scripts README](https://github.com/pixijs/extension-scripts) lists every command and every `extensionConfig` option.

---

# PixiJS 3D

Every template comes with [PixiJS 3D](https://github.com/pixijs/3d), the `@pixi/3d` package. Its `View3D` is a 2D display object that draws a 3D scene into its rectangle, so 3D and 2D share one stage. Each app template draws a lit, spinning cube behind its 2D content to show this.

## How it's set up

- `@pixi/3d` is a dependency next to `pixi.js`. It needs `pixi.js` 8.23.0 or later, which the templates install.
- Importing `@pixi/3d` registers it with PixiJS. `app.init` then loads the 3D code for the renderer it starts, WebGL or WebGPU. Vite, webpack and the import map keep each in its own file, so the browser downloads only the one it uses. The esbuild template bundles both into `bundle.js`.
- Import `@pixi/3d` before `app.init` runs. A `View3D` on an app that started earlier draws nothing. That happens when 3D code is in a file that loads later, so the game templates import `@pixi/3d` at the top of `src/main.ts`. Keep that import when you split your game into files that load on demand.
- The import map template maps `@pixi/3d` and `@pixi/3d/extras` to jsDelivr, next to `pixi.js`.
- The [extension template](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/extension.md) lists `@pixi/3d` as a peer dependency, like `pixi.js`.

## The cube

The bundler templates draw the cube in `src/main.ts`, the React template in the `SpinningCube` component in `src/App.tsx`, and the game templates in `src/cube.ts`. This is the bundler version:

```ts title="src/main.ts"
const view = new View3D({
  autoResize: true,
  environment: { skyColor: 0xc9d6ff, groundColor: 0x3a2f45 },
});

const cube = new Mesh3D({
  geometry: new CubeGeometry(),
  material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xe72264 }),
});

const sun = new DirectionalLight({ intensity: 3 });

sun.position.set(-3, 5, 2);
sun.lookAt(cube.position);

view.root.addChild(cube, sun);
view.camera.position.set(0, 1.6, 3);
view.camera.lookAt(cube.position);
```

- `autoResize` makes the view fill the screen, and keeps it filling the screen when the window resizes. The game templates give the view a fixed `width`, `height` and `anchor` instead, and place it like a sprite. See [the starter game](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/games/starter.md#3d).
- `environment` is soft light from every direction: `skyColor` lights surfaces that face up, and `groundColor` lights surfaces that face down.
- Everything 3D goes under `view.root`, including lights. The view owns its camera.
- Lights and cameras face along their -Z axis. `lookAt` turns them to face a point.
- The view is added to the stage before the bunny, so the bunny draws in front of it. A 2D object added after a view always draws over it. The view also catches pointer events anywhere on screen, so put clickable 2D objects in front of it.
- The camera sits above and in front of the cube, so you see its top as well as its sides.
- The app's ticker turns the cube every frame.

Every app template passes `antialias: true` to `app.init`, which smooths the edges of 3D shapes. `View3D` has no antialias option of its own.

## Extras

`@pixi/3d/extras` has optional pieces, such as camera controls, particles, toon shading and post-processing effects like bloom. For example, to orbit the camera around the cube when you drag, import `OrbitCamera` and create one after the `view.camera` lines:

```ts
import { OrbitCamera } from "@pixi/3d/extras";

new OrbitCamera({ view });
```

`OrbitCamera` reads the view's pointer events. In a game template, change `eventMode` in `src/cube.ts` to `"static"` first. In the React template, keep it in a `const` and call its `destroy()` in the effect's cleanup, or each hot reload adds another controller.

## TypeScript

The app templates' `tsconfig.json` uses the `DOM` library, which in TypeScript 7 leaves out some WebGPU constants, such as `GPUTextureUsage`. If your code uses them, install `@types/web` and use it in place of `DOM` and `DOM.Iterable`, as the [PixiJS 3D README](https://github.com/pixijs/3d#typescript) explains.

## Coding agents

`@pixi/3d` comes with an agent skill in `node_modules/@pixi/3d/skills/pixijs-3d`. It has a complete example for each job, such as loading glTF models, shadows, picking and particles. Point your coding agent at that folder before it writes 3D code.

## Remove it

If your project is 2D only:

1. Delete the cube code and its `@pixi/3d` imports:

   - In a bundler template, the code from `new View3D` to the camera lines in `src/main.ts` or `src/main.js`, `view` in `app.stage.addChild`, and the cube line in the ticker.
   - In the React template, `SpinningCube` and `<SpinningCube />`, the `environment` constant, `View3D` in `extend`, and `src/pixi-react.d.ts`.
   - In a game template, `src/cube.ts`, and in `src/scene.ts` the `createSpinningCube` import and the code that adds the cube.

2. In a game template, delete `import "@pixi/3d"` from `src/main.ts`.

3. Run `npm uninstall @pixi/3d`. In the import map template, delete the two `@pixi/3d` entries from `index.html`.

Only code that imports `@pixi/3d` adds it to a build, so steps 1 and 2 are what make the build smaller.

## Learn more

The [PixiJS 3D repository](https://github.com/pixijs/3d) has a [quick start](https://github.com/pixijs/3d/blob/main/src/__docs__/getting-started/quick-start.md), guides for each part, and examples.

---

# Linting and formatting

Every app template comes with [oxlint](https://oxc.rs/docs/guide/usage/linter) for linting and [oxfmt](https://oxc.rs/docs/guide/usage/formatter) for formatting. Both come from the [Oxc](https://oxc.rs) project and are written in Rust, so they check a whole template in well under a second. A new project passes both with no changes.

The [extension template](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/extension.md) is the exception. It lints with ESLint through `xs lint`.

## Scripts

Lint the project:

**npm**

```bash
npm run lint
```

**yarn**

```bash
yarn lint
```

**pnpm**

```bash
pnpm run lint
```

**bun**

```bash
bun run lint
```

Format every file in place:

**npm**

```bash
npm run format
```

**yarn**

```bash
yarn format
```

**pnpm**

```bash
pnpm run format
```

**bun**

```bash
bun run format
```

`build` runs oxlint first, so a lint error stops the build. Warnings don't.

Two useful variations, shown with npm:

```bash
npm run lint -- --fix   # fix what oxlint can fix on its own
npx oxfmt --check       # list unformatted files without changing them, for CI
```

## Config files

`.oxlintrc.json` turns on the plugins and rules:

```json title=".oxlintrc.json"
{
  "$schema": "./node_modules/oxlint/configuration_schema.json",
  "plugins": ["typescript", "unicorn", "oxc", "import"],
  "env": {
    "browser": true,
    "es2024": true
  },
  "categories": {
    "correctness": "error"
  },
  "rules": {
    "import/no-duplicates": "error",
    "typescript/consistent-type-imports": "error"
  },
  "ignorePatterns": ["dist"]
}
```

- The `correctness` category reports code that is almost certainly a bug, such as unreachable code or a comparison that is always false.
- `import/no-duplicates` flags two import statements for the same module.
- `typescript/consistent-type-imports` asks for `import type` when an import is only used as a type, so bundlers can drop it.

The React template adds the `react` plugin with the `rules-of-hooks`, `exhaustive-deps` and `only-export-components` rules.

For more checks, add a category such as `"suspicious": "warn"` or `"perf": "warn"`, or set single rules under `rules`. The [oxlint rules list](https://oxc.rs/docs/guide/usage/linter/rules) shows every rule and its category.

`.oxfmtrc.json` sets the formatter options:

```json title=".oxfmtrc.json"
{
  "$schema": "./node_modules/oxfmt/configuration_schema.json",
  "printWidth": 80,
  "sortImports": true
}
```

oxfmt formats code the way Prettier does and accepts Prettier's common options, such as `semi`, `singleQuote` and `tabWidth`. `sortImports` sorts and groups import statements.

The `$schema` lines give you autocompletion in editors that read JSON schemas.

## VS Code

`.vscode/extensions.json` recommends the [Oxc extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=oxc.oxc-vscode), `oxc.oxc-vscode`. VS Code offers to install it when you open the project. It shows lint problems as you type.

`.vscode/settings.json` makes the extension the formatter for the project's file types, and formats and applies safe lint fixes when you save:

```json title=".vscode/settings.json"
{
  "[css][html][javascript][javascriptreact][json][jsonc][markdown][typescript][typescriptreact]": {
    "editor.defaultFormatter": "oxc.oxc-vscode"
  },
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "editor.formatOnSaveMode": "file",
  "editor.codeActionsOnSave": {
    "source.fixAll.oxc": "explicit"
  }
}
```

The formatter is set per language so it also wins over language-specific formatters in your user settings, such as Prettier for `[json]`.

The template's `.gitignore` ignores everything in `.vscode/` except these two files.

## Other editors

oxlint and oxfmt work in any editor with language server support, and there are plugins for editors such as Zed and the JetBrains IDEs. See the [Oxc editor setup guide](https://oxc.rs/docs/guide/usage/linter/editors).

## Using ESLint or Prettier instead

The templates run oxlint in `lint` and at the start of `build`, and oxfmt in `format`. To switch, uninstall both, delete their configs and change those scripts.

---

# TypeScript and JavaScript

Most templates come in TypeScript and JavaScript. Choose at the language prompt, or pick the id directly: JavaScript ids end in `-js`, such as `bundler-vite-js`.

- TypeScript and JavaScript: [Game: Starter, Web](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/web.md); [Game: Starter, Web, multiplayer](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/web.md#multiplayer); [Game: Starter, Discord Activity](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md); [Game: Starter, Discord Activity, multiplayer](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md#multiplayer); [Bundler: Vite](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#vite); [Bundler: webpack](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#webpack); [Bundler: esbuild](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#esbuild); [Framework: React](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/react.md)
- TypeScript only: [Extension: Default](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/extension.md)
- JavaScript only: [Bundler: Import map](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#import-map)

## What changes in JavaScript

The JavaScript versions are generated from the TypeScript ones when create-pixi.js is published, so the code is the same apart from the types. Compared with the TypeScript version, a JavaScript project:

- Has `.js` and `.jsx` files instead of `.ts` and `.tsx`, with type annotations removed.
- Has no `tsconfig.json`, no `.d.ts` files and no `typescript` dependency.
- Skips `tsc` in the `build` script, so `build` only lints and bundles.
- Has no `typescript` plugin or rules in `.oxlintrc.json`.

Everything else matches: the bundler config, the dev port, and the oxfmt setup.

## TypeScript version

The app templates use TypeScript 7 and set `noEmit`, so `tsc` only type-checks. Vite, esbuild and esbuild-loader in webpack strip the types when they bundle, which is why `build` runs `tsc` as a separate step. The extension template uses the TypeScript version that comes with Extension Scripts.

`tsconfig.json` turns on `strict` mode and a few extra checks, including `noUnusedLocals` and `noUnusedParameters`. Unused variables and parameters fail the build. Delete them, or prefix an unused parameter with `_`.

## Adding types to a JavaScript project

You can type-check a JavaScript project without converting it. Install TypeScript, add a `jsconfig.json` or `tsconfig.json` with `"checkJs": true`, and describe types with JSDoc comments:

```js
/** @param {import("pixi.js").Sprite} sprite */
function spin(sprite) {
  sprite.rotation += 0.1;
}
```

To move to TypeScript completely, it's usually quicker to create a new project from the TypeScript version of the same template and copy your code across.

---

# CLI reference

```text
create-pixi [OPTION]... [DIRECTORY]
```

With no arguments, create-pixi.js asks for everything it needs. Arguments answer prompts up front.

## Arguments

| Argument           | Description                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DIRECTORY`        | The folder to create the project in. Use `.` for the current folder. When it's left out, the CLI asks, with `pixi-project` as the default.                |
| `-t`, `--template` | The template id. It answers every template prompt. An unknown id shows the template prompts instead.                                                      |
| `--overwrite`      | Answers the prompt for a folder that isn't empty. `yes` removes the existing files, `ignore` keeps them and writes the template on top, and `no` cancels. |
| `-h`, `--help`     | Prints usage and the list of template ids.                                                                                                                |

The folder name also becomes the `name` in `package.json`. If it isn't a valid npm package name, the CLI asks for one.

## Prompts

The CLI asks only what the arguments don't answer. [Answer the prompts](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/installation.md#answer-the-prompts) lists each prompt and when it appears.

## Passing options through a package manager

When you run create-pixi.js through `npm create`, put the options after `--`. Otherwise npm treats them as its own:

**npm**

```bash
npm create pixi.js@latest my-app -- --template bundler-vite
```

**yarn**

```bash
yarn create pixi.js my-app --template bundler-vite
```

**pnpm**

```bash
pnpm create pixi.js my-app --template bundler-vite
```

**bun**

```bash
bun create pixi.js my-app --template bundler-vite
```

To run the CLI without prompts, for example in a script or CI job, pass a folder whose name is a valid package name, the template and, if the folder might not be empty, `--overwrite`:

```bash
npm create pixi.js@latest my-app -- --template bundler-vite --overwrite yes
```

The CLI exits with code 1 if it's cancelled or fails, or if `--overwrite` gets a value other than `yes`, `ignore` or `no`.

You can also run the CLI with `npx create-pixi.js`, or install the `create-pixi.js` package globally and run `create-pixi` or `cpa`. Both take the same options without the extra `--`.

## Template ids

| `--template`                     | Template                                                                                                                  | Language   |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| `starter-web`                    | [Game: Starter, Web](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/web.md)                                           | TypeScript |
| `starter-web-js`                 | [Game: Starter, Web](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/web.md)                                           | JavaScript |
| `starter-web-multiplayer`        | [Game: Starter, Web, multiplayer](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/web.md#multiplayer)                  | TypeScript |
| `starter-web-multiplayer-js`     | [Game: Starter, Web, multiplayer](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/web.md#multiplayer)                  | JavaScript |
| `starter-discord`                | [Game: Starter, Discord Activity](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md)                          | TypeScript |
| `starter-discord-js`             | [Game: Starter, Discord Activity](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md)                          | JavaScript |
| `starter-discord-multiplayer`    | [Game: Starter, Discord Activity, multiplayer](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md#multiplayer) | TypeScript |
| `starter-discord-multiplayer-js` | [Game: Starter, Discord Activity, multiplayer](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md#multiplayer) | JavaScript |
| `bundler-vite`                   | [Bundler: Vite](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#vite)                                                | TypeScript |
| `bundler-vite-js`                | [Bundler: Vite](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#vite)                                                | JavaScript |
| `bundler-webpack`                | [Bundler: webpack](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#webpack)                                          | TypeScript |
| `bundler-webpack-js`             | [Bundler: webpack](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#webpack)                                          | JavaScript |
| `bundler-esbuild`                | [Bundler: esbuild](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#esbuild)                                          | TypeScript |
| `bundler-esbuild-js`             | [Bundler: esbuild](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#esbuild)                                          | JavaScript |
| `bundler-import-map`             | [Bundler: Import map](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#import-map)                                    | JavaScript |
| `framework-react`                | [Framework: React](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/react.md)                                                     | TypeScript |
| `framework-react-js`             | [Framework: React](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/react.md)                                                     | JavaScript |
| `extension-default`              | [Extension: Default](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/extension.md)                                               | TypeScript |

Game template ids are `<game>-<platform>`, plus `-multiplayer` for the multiplayer version and `-js` for JavaScript. See [game templates](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/games.md#pick-a-game-and-a-platform).

## What the CLI writes

The CLI copies the template into the folder, renames `_gitignore` to `.gitignore`, and fills in the `name` field of `package.json`. The extension template also gets `author` in `package.json` and `LICENSE`, read from `git config user.name`. With Yarn 2 or newer, the CLI also writes a `.yarnrc.yml` with `nodeLinker: node-modules`, because TypeScript 7's `tsc` can't resolve packages through Plug'n'Play. It doesn't install dependencies or create a git repository. When it finishes, it prints the next commands for the package manager you used.

---

# Troubleshooting

## pnpm fails with ERR_PNPM_DLX_MULTIPLE_BINS

```text
ERR_PNPM_DLX_MULTIPLE_BINS  Could not determine executable to run. create-pixi.js has multiple binaries: cpa, create-pixi
```

create-pixi.js 1.4.0 and earlier had two commands, `cpa` and `create-pixi`, and `pnpm create` couldn't tell which one to run. Newer versions have a `create-pixi.js` command, named after the package, which is the one pnpm runs. Ask for the latest version:

```bash
pnpm create pixi.js@latest
```

pnpm reuses a package it ran in the last 24 hours. If you still get the error, skip that cache:

```bash
pnpm --config.dlx-cache-max-age=0 create pixi.js@latest
```

To run an older version anyway, name the command yourself: `pnpm --package=create-pixi.js dlx create-pixi`.

## yarn create fails with yarn 1

`yarn create pixi.js` in yarn 1 installs `create-pixi.js` globally and runs a command with the same name. Versions 1.4.0 and earlier didn't have a `create-pixi.js` command, so yarn couldn't find anything to run. Newer versions do.

If you have an old version installed globally, update it, then run the create command again:

```bash
yarn global upgrade create-pixi.js
yarn create pixi.js
```

## Node.js version errors

The templates need Node.js 22.12 or newer, because Vite, oxlint and oxfmt do. The webpack template needs 22.15 or newer for webpack-dev-server 6. On an older version, `npm install` prints `npm warn EBADENGINE Unsupported engine`, and the Vite templates stop with a message that names the Node.js versions Vite supports.

Check your version:

```bash
node --version
```

Install the current LTS release from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/) or through a version manager such as [fnm](https://github.com/Schniz/fnm) or [nvm](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm). Then delete `node_modules` and install again, because some packages download a build for the Node.js version that installed them.

## npm warns about install scripts not covered by allowScripts

```text
npm warn allow-scripts   sharp@0.34.5 (install: node install/check.js || npm run build)
```

npm 11.16 and newer list dependencies whose install scripts aren't covered by `allowScripts` in `package.json`. The templates that use esbuild already allow its script, so you'll usually see this after adding a package such as `sharp`. A new multiplayer project lists `msgpackr-extract`, an optional native add-on that makes Colyseus encode and decode messages faster in Node.js. The scripts still run, and the project works. To stop the warning, approve the packages you trust, which records them in `package.json`:

```bash
npm approve-scripts sharp
```

## npm install fails with spawn git

```text
npm error code ENOENT
npm error syscall spawn git
npm error enoent An unknown git error occurred
```

This happens in a new multiplayer project on a machine without Git. Colyseus lists `@colyseus/uwebsockets-transport` as a peer dependency, so npm installs it too, along with `uWebSockets.js`, which comes from GitHub instead of the npm registry. The template doesn't use it, but npm needs [Git](https://git-scm.com/downloads) to look up that version the first time. Install Git, then run `npm install` again. Once the project has a `package-lock.json`, `npm ci` works without Git.

## Importing GLSL shader files

You don't need a plugin to load shaders in the game, Vite and React templates. Add `?raw` to the import and Vite gives you the file contents as a string:

```ts
import { Filter, GlProgram } from "pixi.js";

import fragment from "./shaders/wave.frag?raw";
import vertex from "./shaders/wave.vert?raw";

const filter = new Filter({
  glProgram: new GlProgram({ vertex, fragment }),
});
```

TypeScript already knows the type of `?raw` imports through `src/vite-env.d.ts`. See [importing an asset as a string](https://vite.dev/guide/assets#importing-asset-as-string) in the Vite docs. For shader `#include` support, the [vite-plugin-glsl](https://github.com/UstymUkhman/vite-plugin-glsl) plugin is an option.

## A View3D draws nothing

The app started before `@pixi/3d` was imported, so its renderer has no 3D code. This happens when 3D code is in a file that loads after `app.init`. Import `@pixi/3d` at the top of your entry file, as [PixiJS 3D](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/pixijs-3d.md#how-its-set-up) shows. With an import map, load `pixi.js` only through the map, not a `<script>` tag.

## The dev server port is already in use

Something else is using port 8080. Stop it, or [change the dev server port](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/bundlers.md#change-the-dev-server-port).

## Discord Activity problems

The Discord guide has its own [troubleshooting](https://pixijs.io/create-pixi/docs/guide/platforms/discord.md#troubleshooting) section, for an Activity that stays blank, sign-in that fails, and an app missing from the App Launcher.

## Something else

Search the [issues on GitHub](https://github.com/pixijs/create-pixi/issues), or ask in the [PixiJS Discord](https://discord.gg/CPTjeb28nH).

---

# Contributing

create-pixi.js lives at [github.com/pixijs/create-pixi](https://github.com/pixijs/create-pixi). Bug reports, template fixes and docs changes are all welcome.

## Set up the repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/pixijs/create-pixi.git
cd create-pixi
npm install
npm run build
npm test
```

You need Node.js 22.18 or newer to run the TypeScript build scripts. `npm run build` builds the CLI and generates every template into `dist/templates/`. Run the built CLI with `npm start`.

## How templates are made

The templates aren't stored as finished projects. Each one is put together from shared layers when the package is built, so a file that several templates use lives in one place. `templates/manifest.ts` lists every template and its layers, and `templates/package.json` holds every dependency version.

Game templates aren't listed one by one. The manifest lists games, in `templates/layers/games/`, and platforms, in `templates/layers/platforms/`, and puts every game on every platform, with a multiplayer version when both the game and the platform have one.

The CLI prompts, its `--help` output and the template lists on this site all read from `templates/manifest.ts`.

[templates/README.md](https://github.com/pixijs/create-pixi/blob/main/templates/README.md) explains how layers combine, how the JavaScript versions are generated, and how to add a template, a game or a platform.

## Try a template while you edit it

```bash
npm run play -- bundler-vite
```

This generates the template into `playground/bundler-vite`, installs its dependencies, starts its dev server, and regenerates the template when files in `templates/layers` change.

To check a template the way CI does, scaffold it with the built CLI, install, lint, check formatting and build:

```bash
npm run verify -- bundler-vite framework-react-js
```

## Work on these docs

The site is in `docs/` and uses [Docusaurus](https://docusaurus.io). From the repository root:

```bash
npm run start:docs
```

Pages are in `docs/docs/guide/`. The [docs README](https://github.com/pixijs/create-pixi/blob/main/docs/README.md) has the build and deploy commands.
